items.title: Driver and conductor killed as Kozhikode-Bengaluru KSRTC bus overturns near Bidadi
items.summary: Two people were killed and 25 others injured after a Kerala State Road Transport Corporation (KSRTC) bus travelling to Bengaluru overturned after crashing into a directional signboard on the Bengaluru-Mysuru Highway near Avaragere Gate in Bengaluru South district on Saturday, August 8. The deceased have been identified as Mithan and Arun Kumar, the conductor and driver of the bus, respectively. Both were from Kerala and were in their 40s. A senior police officer from Bidadi said one of the 25 injured passengers is in critical condition after suffering severe head injuries. The accident occurred around 6.30 am when the bus veered to the left and rammed into a directional signboard before overturning. A passenger alerted the police, following which personnel from the Bidadi police and fire department launched a rescue operation. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment. Several passengers suffered injuries to their hands, legs and upper body, though most were reported to be out of danger. Police suspect the driver may have felt drowsy, as the bus veered sharply toward the side of the road, indicating a possible loss of control. However, officials said the exact cause of the accident would be established after a detailed investigation. The Bidadi police have registered an FIR under the relevant provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) relating to causing death by negligence. The bodies of the driver and conductor have been kept at nearby hospitals, and their families have been informed. The bodies will be handed over to their families after they arrive in Bengaluru. Traffic on the highway was briefly disrupted after debris from the bus fell onto the road, posing a risk to other motorists. Police and emergency personnel cleared the debris and restored traffic movement, the officer said.

items.title: Refurbished vs New Laptops in India: Which Is the Better Deal in 2026?
items.summary: Every online laptop listing looks compelling until you try to untangle the warranty terms. Refurbished devices often undercut new prices by a meaningful margin, but what you save upfront can disappear quickly if battery capacity fades or after-sales support falls short. This guide walks through what actually separates a sound purchase from a stressful one. Refurbished vs New: How the Real Difference Plays Out The price gap between a refurbished and a new laptop can look significant sometimes, ₹10,000 to ₹20,000 on the same model. But the comparison does not end at the sticker price. What you give up with refurbished: A refurbished laptop has a usage history. That history is invisible to you at the time of purchase. Battery health degrades with charge cycles, and most refurbished listings do not state this clearly. Cosmetic condition grades like "Grade A" or "like new" vary significantly by seller and carry no standardised definition in India. Accessories (charger, documentation, original box) may or may not be included. And critically, the warranty is almost always seller-backed rather than manufacturer-backed, which means your recourse after seven days depends entirely on that seller's willingness to cooperate. What you give up with the new: Primarily, money. A new laptop at ₹55,000 may be available refurbished for ₹38,000 to ₹42,000. For buyers with tight budgets and light usage needs, that gap is real and meaningful. New laptops also depreciate the moment they leave the box. If you plan to resell within a year or two, a refurbished device bought at a lower price may leave you in a similar position. Where refurbished makes sense: Refurbished laptops are a reasonable choice when the seller clearly states battery health percentage, condition grade with a specific definition, warranty duration and coverage scope, return terms beyond seven days, and how faults are handled post-delivery. When all of that is transparent and documented, a refurbished device from a credible seller can represent genuine value. When any of it is vague, the savings are not worth the uncertainty. Where new makes more sense: For students who need reliable software compatibility, professionals who cannot afford downtime, or first-time buyers who are not comfortable verifying technical specs independently, a new laptop removes the pre-purchase variables entirely. items.title: Bengaluru cops detain hundreds of people in ‘illegal migrant’ drive, activists accuse assault
items.summary: Hours after Bengaluru Police launched a citywide drive to identify suspected illegal immigrants, a group of civil liberties organisations has accused the force of illegally detaining and assaulting hundreds of migrant workers, including women and children. In a complaint to the Karnataka Home Minister, the Peoples Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL), All India Lawyers Association for Justice (AILAJ), Domestic Workers Rights Union (DWRU), and All India Central Council of Trade Unions (AICCTU) alleged that police teams entered slum settlements across the city early Saturday, August 8, detaining people in the name of identifying Bangladeshi nationals. They said the people detained were predominantly poor, daily-wage and migrant workers. According to the complaint, police entered homes between 6:30 and 7:30 am and, even after residents produced identity documents, forced some into police vehicles and took them to police stations, convention centres and marriage halls. Lawyers and activists from the four organisations visited these sites and spoke with detainees and officials. At Varthur, 41 people, including women, were detained, and at least six alleged they were beaten with lathis, among them a 60-year-old man, a man who was already injured and unwell, and a 30-year-old who reportedly sustained serious injuries after being beaten by four officers. At Bandepalya, more than 200 people, including women and children, were detained across four settlements, while at Hebbagodi, around 150 people were detained, and police allegedly broke down doors and CCTV equipment, with activists saying they personally saw more than 50 phones confiscated. At Parappana Agrahara, more than 400 people were detained across four localities, with phones confiscated and a group of 20 people locked in a separate room as suspected foreign nationals. Smaller numbers were reported elsewhere: around 75 people detained at Somasundrapalya, around 40 at HAL, four at Whitefield, 15 at Mahadevapura, and around 30 at Marathahalli. The organisations also alleged that police seized phones and examined private messages and call logs, objecting to people being referred to the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) based solely on international numbers in call records, arguing this doesn't establish foreign citizenship. items.title: Telangana School Education Dept says private schools must make fee details public
items.summary: Follow TNM's WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. The Telangana School Education Department has instructed private unaided schools to make their fee structures for the 2026–27 academic year publicly available to parents and students. Under the latest directions, schools must display class-wise fee details at their campuses and publish the same information on their official websites. The fee details must also be uploaded to the Telangana School Education Department’s official portal, schooledu.telangana.gov.in. Telangana state director of school education E Naveen Nicolas said Regional Joint Directors and District Educational Officers have been asked to ensure that private unaided schools comply with the directions. The department has created a dedicated facility on its portal through which school managements can submit their fee details. Schools are also required to upload the documents used to arrive at the fee amounts for each class. These supporting records must be signed by members of the school’s governing body and prepared in accordance with the provisions of the relevant 1994 Government Order. The GO enacted the Andhra Pradesh Educational Institutions (Establishment, Recognition, Administration and Control of Schools under Private Managements) Rules, 1993/1994, which continue to regulate private school operations, governance, and fee structures in Telangana post the bifurcation of the Telugu states. The department said the move is intended to improve transparency and ensure that parents have clear access to information on the fees being collected by private unaided schools. Authorities have also warned schools against non-compliance. Schools that fail to display their fee structure on their notice boards and websites may receive show-cause notices from the concerned Regional Joint Directors or District Educational Officers.
